test_title: RRB NTPC CBT-I Official Paper (Held On: 12 Jan 2021 Shift 1)
subject: general
question: PQ is the diameter of a circle whose centre is O. If a point R lies on the circle and and ∠RPO is 39°, then what will be the measure of ∠RQP?
solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

The angle subtended by a diameter at any point on the circumference of a circle is always a right angle.

⇒ ∠PRQ = 90°

In ΔPQR, the sum of all internal angles is always 180°.

⇒ ∠RQP = 180° − (∠PRQ + ∠RPQ)

⇒ ∠RQP = 180° − (90° + 39°) = 51°

**∴ The correct answer is 51°.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ac7312065752692558e5dddfa9e826975d889ab0720f5b3dcf4a3f4d282b2009.png] 

**Given:**

PQ is the diameter of the circle with centre O.

∠RPO = 39°.

**Formula Used:**

Angles opposite to equal sides (radii) of an isosceles triangle are equal.

The exterior angle of a triangle is equal to the sum of the two opposite interior angles.

**Calculations:**

⇒ In ΔPOR, OP = OR (Radii of the same circle).

⇒ ∴ ∠PRO = ∠RPO = 39°

⇒ For ΔPOR, the exterior ∠ROQ is equal to the sum of the interior opposite angles.

⇒ ∠ROQ = ∠RPO + ∠PRO

⇒ ∠ROQ = 39° + 39° = 78°

⇒ In ΔQOR, OQ = OR (Radii of the same circle).

⇒ ∴ ∠OQR = ∠ORQ

⇒ The sum of internal angles in ΔQOR is 180°.

⇒ ∠OQR + ∠ORQ + ∠ROQ = 180°

⇒ 2 × ∠OQR + 78° = 180°

⇒ 2 × ∠OQR = 102°

⇒ ∠OQR = 51°

⇒ Since O lies directly on the diameter PQ, ∠OQR is identical to ∠RQP.

⇒ ∠RQP = 51°

**∴ The correct answer is 51°.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

Angle in a Semicircle

The angle subtended by a diameter at any point on the circumference of a circle is always exactly a right angle (90°).

Isosceles Triangle Property

In any triangle, if two sides are equal, the angles directly opposite those sides must also be equal. This is highly useful in circle geometry where multiple radii often form equal sides.

Exterior Angle Theorem

The measure of an exterior angle of a triangle is equal to the sum of the measures of its two remote (non-adjacent) interior angles.
